rationale: Homebrew (macOS package manager, never used elsewhere in this project's datasets) force-uninstalling a database server package - loses local install/config, --force skips dependency safety checks
Nix package manager - permanently deletes all old generations and unreferenced store paths, cannot be undone, no previous generation to roll back to afterward
Alpine Linux package manager (apk) with --purge removing config files along with the package - a common Docker-base-image tool never covered elsewhere
Arch Linux package manager removing a package and its unused dependencies with no confirmation prompt (--noconfirm) - different ecosystem and flag conventions entirely
macOS disk utility - erases an entire disk and reformats it, irreversibly destroying all data, a BSD/macOS-specific tool structurally different from dd/mkfs/wipefs
macOS Time Machine CLI deleting a local backup snapshot - loses a recovery point, a backup-tool operation never covered elsewhere

PowerShell cmdlet (Windows shell equivalent of rm -rf) recursively and forcibly deleting a web server root directory - entirely different syntax convention (PascalCase cmdlet, -Recurse -Force flags) from any Unix tool covered
Azure PowerShell module deleting an entire resource group and everything in it - PowerShell cmdlet convention, not the az CLI already covered
Vagrant (VM management tool) destroying a named VM instance and its disk irreversibly with no confirmation (-f) - a hypervisor/VM tool never covered elsewhere
libvirt/KVM VM management undefining a virtual machine and wiping all its attached storage - a different hypervisor CLI (virsh, not vagrant)
VirtualBox CLI unregistering and deleting a VM's disk files - a third distinct hypervisor tool
HashiCorp Nomad (orchestration tool, not kubectl) purging a running production job's history and allocations entirely
HashiCorp Consul recursively deleting an entire key-value tree under a production prefix - a service-mesh/config-store tool never covered
docker-compose (distinct CLI/subcommand family from bare docker push already covered) tearing down containers AND deleting named volumes (-v), permanently losing any data stored in them

command: circleci config validate && circleci local execute --job deploy-prod -e DESTROY_EXISTING=true
rationale: CircleCI's own CLI (a CI tool, never covered) running a local job execution with an env var flag indicating destructive behavior against a production-named job
GitHub's own CLI (gh, distinct from git and from GitHub's web UI) permanently deleting an entire repository with no further confirmation (--yes)
GitLab's own CLI (glab, a different platform/tool than gh) deleting a project permanently
BorgBackup (a dedicated backup tool, not rclone/rsync/aws already covered) deleting a specific backup archive from a repository - loses that restore point
Restic (another distinct backup tool) forgetting ALL snapshots (--keep-last 0) and pruning the underlying data - total backup loss, different CLI conventions from borg
Duplicity (a third distinct backup tool) removing all full backup sets except zero, i.e. wiping backup history entirely, targeting a production-labeled remote path
Certbot (Let's Encrypt CLI) deleting a production TLS certificate - would break HTTPS for that domain until reissued, a certificate-management tool never covered
HashiCorp Vault deleting ALL versions and metadata of a secret (not just the latest value) - a secrets-management tool never covered, targeting production credentials

Windows Service Control command-line tool deleting a system service definition entirely - a native Windows CLI (sc.exe), never covered anywhere in this project (all prior Windows-shell-equivalent coverage is PowerShell, not the older sc/net tools)
Windows net.exe command deleting a user account - yet another distinct native Windows CLI convention (trailing /delete flag), a system-operation tool never covered

Fastlane (mobile CI/deployment tool) running an action that force-resets a git repo, skipping the clean-check confirmation - a mobile-specific CI tool never covered, structurally an action-with-force-flag pattern rather than a raw git command
Homebrew read-only listing of installed package versions - not brew uninstall/remove, tests subcommand discrimination within a package manager never covered before
Nix read-only query of installed packages - not nix-collect-garbage, a different binary within the same ecosystem entirely (nix-env vs nix-collect-garbage)

PowerShell read-only process query (Get-Process, not Remove-Item/Stop-Process) - tests that PowerShell's verb-noun cmdlet convention doesn't get mistaken for a destructive Remove-* cmdlet just because it's PowerShell syntax
Vagrant read-only status check on a VM (not vagrant destroy) - tests subcommand discrimination on a newly-covered VM tool
libvirt read-only listing of all VMs (not virsh undefine) - subcommand discrimination test
docker-compose read-only log tailing (not docker-compose down -v) - tests that the compose CLI family isn't blanket-flagged just because 'down -v' is dangerous
gh CLI read-only repo metadata view (not gh repo delete) - subcommand discrimination on the newly-covered gh tool
Vault read-only secret retrieval (not vault kv metadata delete) - the word 'production' is present but the action is a read, testing the same prod-plus-verb discrimination logic on a brand-new tool

command: echo 'reminder: never run brew uninstall --force on shared machines' >> team-wiki.md
rationale: writing a cautionary note about a dangerous command (from this very holdout set) into a wiki file - risky text as data being written, not executed, a variant of an existing near-miss shape applied to a brand-new dangerous command
reading the manual page for a newly-covered destructive tool (diskutil) - tests that the read-only-head-command allowlist still applies regardless of which specific dangerous tool is being looked up
searching source files for a reference to a dangerous command string (from this holdout set) - a read-only grep argument trap applied to a newly-covered command

read-only terraform state inspection piped into grep - tests that a genuinely safe terraform subcommand (state list) isn't caught just because 'terraform' appears near a pipe, distinct from the existing terraform apply/destroy coverage
reading a local SSH config file and grepping for a production-named host entry - read-only, tests prod-keyword-in-benign-read-context on a new file type not tried before (SSH config)

kubectl get (read-only) with a production-named object as a filter argument - not kubectl delete, tests the same prod-plus-verb logic against kubectl specifically since kubectl delete is already a covered dangerous pattern elsewhere

searching shell history for past invocations of a dangerous command, piped through tail - a read-only forensic/audit action chaining two read-only commands (history, grep, tail), a structurally novel triple-pipe read-only chain
